item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Genus groupings reflect similarity of biology, which is not quite the same thing as evolutionary "family tree". … There is no reason that an alien species with sufficient convergent evolution couldn't be designated "homo".

Um, what? While the field of taxonomy technically does not include phylogenetics or vice versa, modern taxonomists almost universally work from an evolutionary standpoint, even if their species concepts vary. While phenetics and numerical taxonomy do have a place today, data from phylogenetic systematics dominate nearly every decision made with regard to revising modern taxonomy, even tentative taxonomic placement (which would include extraterrestrial life).

I will grant that, once upon a time, clades (at the genus or any other level) were crafted based on morphological or other similarity. I will also grant that the designation of one genus from another is somewhat arbitrary, again based on gross dissimilarity from other, related genera.

However, the science of taxonomy, starting with Linneaus, is hierarchical. One of Darwin's greatest triumphs with Origin was to show why a hierarchical taxonomy made sense: because it is a natural result of common descent.

If the author of this entry wants to leave it open to interpretation as to the origin of the Gray Guy, that's his/her place to do so. If they wished to imply alien more heavily, I submit they use a new, currently nonexistant genus, as per the International Codes of Zoological and Botanical Nomenclature.* Homonoides ("man-like") is unfortunately already claimed by a genus of moths, so perhaps Xenohomo ("stranger/foreign man") or similar would work.

*Though technically neither of these codes applies because an alien, not being descendent from the ancestor of Earth animals or plants, is neither.

Not necessarily. Genus groupings reflect similarity of biology, which is not quite the same thing as evolutionary "family tree".

There is no established naming protocol for extra-terrestrial species, so there is no reason that an alien species with sufficient convergent evolution couldn't be designated "homo".

Alternatively, since H. Ignotus is a black box at this point, it could also just as well be that they actually are an off-shoot of humanity, divergently evolved after leaving Earth sometime in pre-history.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I am so torn on this one.

I love the set up. You did a great job giving flavor to the containment procedures; I especially loved the bit about having to have a non-standard cover story due to the instability in the Congo. Great work there.

However, once you get to what the SCP actually does, it lets me down. So…aliens are re-arranging internal organs? Whooptie do. Why should I, the reader, care? A good SCP needs to be either A) scary, B) very interesting, or C) very, very, very clever. This isn't enough of any of these. I don't find myself particularly frightened by it, and the effect isn't terribly interesting. I also agree with what others said that the bit about the alien was kind of weak. It may be workable, but it isn't fleshed out enough for us to get what you are going for.

In the end, I have to give this a loud, resounding no-vote. Good setup, but the SCP itself lets me down.

Also, what is the deal with the room? How are they "appearing" in it? Can't we just put cameras in there and see exactly what is going on at all times? Are they materializing? Are they getting teleported in? Do they start as larva and grow into cocoons? You have a big gap in the story there that could be neat, but you never even mention it.

item.content:encoded:
Nicely realized setting. Interesting development of the anomoly, various creatures are OHGODOHGODLAND-HAGFISHKILLITKILLITAAAAAAAHH!!!

*ahem*

Clean, tightly written, good wordcraft (if I can use that term without sounding even more pretentious than usual). I don't usually have time to get to the "The act of reading is now subconcious, you are experiencing the story in your head" stage of immersion in pieces this short, but I did here.

The picture of the disembodied head had kind of a "Mordo, Master of the Dark Forces/third-tier Vegas show" feel to it, but the other images worked fine and Mordo didn't jar me enough to knock me out of the groove.

The off-list SCP ("alien") was, as you observed, a risk, but it was handled deftly enough as an "eyes-only" extra that I felt it worked well.

Overall: A fine specimen of an SCP. Moar plz.

+1
